subChunks.title: UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT
subChunks.hookHtml: Sometimes you need to stack the results of two queries vertically — adding rows together rather than joining tables horizontally. UNION does exactly that.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
UNION — combine and deduplicate

SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice'
UNION
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE xp > 4000;

Rules: both queries must return the same number of columns, and column types must be compatible. UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result.

UNION ALL — keep duplicates

SELECT name FROM table_a
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM table_b;

UNION ALL is faster than UNION because it skips the deduplication step. Prefer it when you know the results are distinct or when duplicates are acceptable.

INTERSECT — rows in both results

SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE xp > 1000
INTERSECT
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank != 'Mage';

EXCEPT — rows in the first but not the second

SELECT name FROM apprentices
EXCEPT
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice';

INTERSECT and EXCEPT are in the SQL standard but not all engines support them (MySQL added INTERSECT only in v8.0.31).

storyBeats.text: Two ledgers from different Academy buildings — the Archivist must combine them into a single list with no duplicates.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: UNION stacks two result sets vertically and removes duplicates. UNION ALL stacks them without removing anything — faster, but you must be sure duplicates are acceptable. INTERSECT gives only rows appearing in both; EXCEPT gives rows in the first but absent from the second.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Combined list

Return the names of all apprentices who are either rank 'Novice' OR have XP above 4 000, using UNION (no duplicates). Order by name.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice'
UNION
SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE xp > 4000
ORDER BY name;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns 3 rows (Dorian Novice, Cassia xp>4000, Elara xp>4000)
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800),(4,'Dorian','Novice',80),(5,'Elara','Archmage',7500),(6,'Fenrir','Apprentice',950);

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns Cassia, Dorian, Elara (alphabetically)
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' UNION SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE xp > 4000 ORDER BY name

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Using EXCEPT, return the names of apprentices who have XP over 500 but are NOT rank 'Apprentice'. Order by name.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between UNION and UNION ALL, and when you would choose each one.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
options: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates
UNION ALL removes duplicates; UNION keeps all rows
UNION joins horizontally; UNION ALL stacks vertically
UNION ALL requires matching column names; UNION does not
questions.answer: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates
questions.explanation: Both stack result sets vertically. UNION does an implicit DISTINCT over the combined results (more expensive). UNION ALL skips deduplication and is therefore faster.

questions.prompt: Using lesson data, how many rows does the UNION query in the guided practice return?
questions.explanation: First query: rank='Novice' → Dorian. Second query: xp>4000 → Cassia (4800), Elara (7500). UNION combines and deduplicates: 3 distinct rows.

questions.prompt: What must be true for two queries to be combined with UNION?
options: Both must return the same number of columns with compatible types
Both must query the same table
Both must have the same WHERE clause
Both must return at least one row
questions.answer: Both must return the same number of columns with compatible types
questions.explanation: UNION stacks rows. For stacking to work, each row must have the same shape — same column count and compatible types. The column names in the result are taken from the first query.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer UNION ALL over UNION?
options: When you know the results are already distinct, or duplicates are acceptable — UNION ALL is faster
When you need duplicates removed automatically
When the two queries return different column counts
questions.answer: When you know the results are already distinct, or duplicates are acceptable — UNION ALL is faster
questions.explanation: UNION performs a sort/hash to deduplicate, which has a cost. UNION ALL skips that step. If your data is already distinct by design, or duplicates are harmless, always prefer UNION ALL for performance.
